title: Verbs and Modals
shortDescription: Action words, linking verbs, and the modal verbs (can/could/must/should...) that carry meaning exams test constantly.
genZNote: Verbs run the sentence engine. Modals are the engine's mood settings — possibility, obligation, permission, all in one small word.

rows: Needs a direct object to complete its meaning
She IS a doctor. / He SEEMS happy.
Connects subject to a description, not an action
She IS reading. / They HAVE gone.
Supports the main verb to form tense/voice/questions
You MUST leave. / She CAN swim.

sections.heading: Linking verbs vs action verbs — the adjective-after-verb trap
sections.body: After a linking verb (be, seem, become, appear, and sense-verbs like feel/look/smell/taste/sound when describing a state), you need an ADJECTIVE, not an adverb: 'The soup tastes GOOD' (not 'well', unless describing the sense of taste itself working properly). After an action verb, you generally need an adverb: 'He tasted the soup CAREFULLY.' The exam trick is telling whether the verb is being used as a linking verb (describing the subject) or an action verb (describing how something is done).

sections.heading: Common modal verbs and their core meanings

rows: Ability, permission (informal); could = past ability or polite request
She can swim. / Could you help me?
Permission (formal), possibility; might = weaker possibility than may
You may leave. / It might rain.
You must submit by Friday. / He must be tired (deduction).
Future intention/certainty; would = past habit, polite/conditional
I will call you. / He would visit every summer.
Formal future (with I/we), suggestions/offers in questions
Absence of obligation (not the same as 'must not')
You needn't come if you're busy.

sections.heading: Modal verb exam traps
bullets: 'Must not' means it is PROHIBITED; 'need not' means it is simply NOT REQUIRED — these are opposite in force and are a classic confusion pair.
Modals are never followed by 'to' + verb in their basic form: say 'can swim', never 'can to swim'; the exception is 'ought TO' and 'have TO', which behave like modals but do take 'to'.
Modals do not take -s in the third person: 'he can', never 'he cans'.
Two modals cannot be stacked together in standard English: 'might can' or 'must should' are incorrect.

sections.heading: Verb forms and phrasal verbs, briefly
sections.body: Every regular verb has five forms an exam may test indirectly through tense questions: base (walk), -s form (walks), -ing form (walking), past (walked), past participle (walked). Irregular verbs (go/went/gone, eat/ate/eaten) must be memorised individually since they don't follow the -ed pattern. A phrasal verb combines a verb with a particle to create a new meaning distinct from the verb alone — 'give up' (quit) is not related in meaning to 'give'; exams sometimes test recognising the idiomatic meaning of common phrasal verbs like 'look after' (take care of), 'put off' (postpone), and 'run into' (meet unexpectedly).

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Verbs show action or state of being; modal auxiliary verbs (can, must, should, may...) attach to a main verb to express ability, permission, obligation, or possibility.
keyFacts: Linking verbs are followed by an adjective describing the subject, not an adverb.
'Must not' = prohibited; 'need not' = simply not required — opposite meanings.
Modals never take -s or a following bare 'to' (except ought to, have to).

highYieldFacts: 'He can to speak English' is wrong — modals are followed directly by the base verb.
'You must not smoke here' (prohibited) is very different from 'You need not smoke here' (optional).
commonTraps: Adding -s to a modal: 'she cans drive'.
Using an adverb after a linking verb: 'The cake tastes deliciously' should be 'tastes delicious'.
mustRemember: Identify whether the verb links back to the subject (needs adjective) or describes an action (can take adverb).

confusedTerms.distinction: 'Must not' expresses prohibition (you are not allowed to). 'Need not' expresses absence of obligation (you are allowed to skip it, but it's not forbidden).

possibleQuestions: Spot the error: 'You needn't smoke in this compartment; it is a criminal offence.' (should be 'must not')
Choose the correct verb form after the linking verb: 'The milk has gone ___ (bad/badly).'
